title: Looking for the body
hookLine: search the body part by part; where is "the body"? (Bodhicaryavatara 9)
tomorrow: no body found. so who's doing the looking?

cards: Point to your body. Most likely your finger went to your chest. But that's your chest.
We say my body all day without checking what we mean. Is the body your hand? Your shins?
Your back? Shantideva runs this exact search himself, part by part, in the Bodhicaryavatara, and the result is a little dizzying. It sounds like a riddle.

teach.h: NOT THE FEET, NOT THE SHINS.
teach.b: The body isn't the feet, he says, or the shins, or the thighs, or the hips, the belly, the back, the chest, the arms. If the body were in each part, there'd be many bodies; if it's apart from them, where is it?

Look as long as you like and you find parts. 'Body' is the name the mind lays over them, the way the eye sees a person in a post at dusk. He isn't saying your body doesn't matter, or that pain isn't real.
Conventionally, you have a body, and you feed it and care for it.
Ultimately, you can't find a body standing apart from its parts. It's the same move as taking away the table's legs and top, only now the table is you.
That's yesterday's two truths, made personal. Now the week, gathered. Travelers at an inn: love with an open hand.
Just as I do. One body. Exchange.
And today's question, which sends the search inward: where is it?

how: Buddhist meditators across schools practice body scans and analytical meditation, moving attention through the body's parts; in Tibetan study this search prepares the search for the self.

games.q: what does “looking for the body” mean?
o: a medical checkup that goes from head to toe
forgetting the body so that the mind can rest
searching the body part by part and finding no body

p: part by part, feet to face
a name laid over the parts
you still feed and care for it

s: Shantideva finds the body in the feet or the shins
he goes through the parts and finds no body in any one of them.
for Shantideva, the body isn't real at all, so it doesn't need care
conventionally you have a body to feed and care for; the search is about the ultimate.
the search for the body puts the two truths to work

games.q: your friend worries: 'if there's no body apart from the parts, does my pain even count?' what's a fair reply from today?
o: it counts: conventionally your body and pain are real; the search is about how things exist.
no, pain is an illusion, so it shouldn't bother you.
Shantideva never meant any of this for real bodies.
games.why: the two truths hold together: the pain is real in the everyday world, and the search looks at how the body exists.

practice: Close your eyes and move your attention slowly upward: feet, shins, knees, thighs, belly, chest, arms, face. At each stop, ask gently: is this the body? Then rest your attention on the whole, and notice what's there.

wordCard.voice: Looking for the body: Shantideva's search, part by part, for the body itself. Parts are found; a body apart from them isn't.

carryVoice: Your line: where is it? Asked kindly, by a body that still needs feeding. Two weeks, gathered.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 9.78-9.87 (the body is not the feet, shins, thighs...; like seeing a person in a post)
